target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove work-based voting barriers for many Americans
objection: A federal Election Day holiday does not require private employers to give paid time off, so many low-income workers in retail and service jobs would still have to work and would not reliably gain time to vote.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday would broadly increase access and turnout
objection: Because a holiday would not reliably remove the main practical barriers for low-income voters, any turnout or access gains would be limited and uneven rather than broadly beneficial.

target: AG1's claim that an Election Day holiday is a useful voting-access reform on its own
objection: Research shows that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1's comparison of a holiday to other reforms
objection: State laws requiring employer time off for voting and automatic voter registration are more direct and reliable ways to improve voting access than creating a federal holiday.

target: AG2's claim that a national holiday would not reliably remove work-based barriers for low-income workers
objection: Even without a legal requirement for paid time off, national holidays commonly cause many schools and employers to close or reduce schedules, so a holiday would in practice reduce work-based voting barriers for many low-income workers.

target: AG2's claim that low-income workers would be disadvantaged because the holiday would not reliably help them
objection: If a policy reduces required work obligations and creates more daytime availability to vote, it can help workers who have hourly schedules and limited flexibility, even if employers are not legally required to provide paid leave.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday would not be worthwhile unless it perfectly solved every access problem
objection: A policy is still worth supporting if it removes major scheduling barriers for many people, even if it is not perfectly effective for every voter.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday would disadvantage low-income voters by disrupting school and child-care routines
objection: National holidays typically reduce school and child-care scheduling barriers, which can help working parents and low-income households rather than harming them.

target: AG2's assumption that reduced school and child-care schedules would likely hurt low-income voters more than others
objection: Because low-income households include people with school-age children and face school-related supervision constraints, it is not justified to assume the holiday would likely disadvantage them; it may instead improve their access to voting.

target: AG2's argument that a holiday would not help because polling logistics are the real issue
objection: Many polling places are in public facilities such as schools and community buildings, and a national holiday would reduce conflicts with those facilities' normal schedules, making polling locations easier to keep open and staffed.

target: AG2's claim that polling-site or staffing disruptions make a holiday ineffective for low-income workers
objection: More reliable polling-site operations on Election Day would reduce delays and missed opportunities, which especially helps voters who cannot easily rearrange work schedules, including many low-income workers.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would be a useful standalone reform
objection: A federal Election Day holiday would likely consume limited legislative and administrative attention, crowding out or slowing other voting-access reforms that are more effective.

target: AG2's claim that low-income households would be disadvantaged because school and child-care routines would be disrupted
objection: Low-income households are often the ones most constrained by inflexible schedules, so reducing school and child-care barriers would relieve rather than worsen their ability to vote.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would reduce school and child-care barriers without creating new burdens
objection: If normal school and child-care services are disrupted, households that rely on them must arrange alternative supervision or alter their own work schedules, which adds time and cost burdens.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday would help low-income voters rather than hurt them
objection: Because low-income households are less able to absorb extra time and cost burdens from disrupted child-care or school routines, a holiday can actually interfere with their ability to vote.
